narrative:
Welcome to July in September, everyone. Mid-summer heat & humidity are at their worst today through Friday, with record or near-record highs expected. Only a rogue afternoon shower or two manages to pop today, leaving most hot and dry. Coverage increases a bit starting Thursday, but still only widely scattered as we move into the weekend. Temperatures back off some Saturday, and further relief follows.

The Monday Message is back today for our subscribers! We have a hot week, yielding to a cooler Labor Day holiday weekend.

Subscribe Forecast Discussion Unpleasant heat dominates the headlines for the next three days, as we await the arrival of a front from the north on Saturday. Just a rogue shower or two may manage to exist today, likely south of Ashe County if at all. Afternoon shower coverage recovers some beginning Thursday, staying at “widely scattered” levels into the weekend. The heat building in is a rarity… should Boone manage to hit 85 degrees each day through Friday as we expect, it will be the first time in 72 years that there has been four consecutive highs of 85 or greater in September. Saturday could be close to 85 as well, depending on PM shower activity. As the hot upper-level ridge overhead loosens its grip, a weakness develops and allows for the aforementioned front to come through to start the weekend. You won’t feel much relief until Sunday, which is a step cooler, but Monday brings drier air in with highs finally sinking back below 80. Showers and perhaps some fog develops along and east of the Blue Ridge Sunday evening into Labor Day as ESE flow sets up with high pressure to the north. That flow lingers into Tuesday, keeping a couple of light showers around. Temperatures begin to warm back up into the middle of next week. Submitted by Ellen Carpenter. All Photos Submit Photo Latest Insights August 2026 Recap First Weekend Flooding The story all spring and into the beginning of summer had been dry, dry, dry. Drought was just about the only weather story for the first third of summer, but July and August have bucked that trend with gusto. After July ended rather wet, the first weekend of August brought home isolated pockets of 5"+ for a handful of locations across the Ray's Weather coverage region. The most notable pocket of rain was in northeastern Surry County, where 8-10"+ fell on the 1st and 2nd, producing destructive flash flooding in Mount Airy. The city's public works fleet sustained several million dollars worth of damage from the fast-rising floodwaters, and a handful of nearby businesses experienced damage as well. Blowing Rock also saw brief flash flooding that weekend, with training thunderstorms (storms repeatedly moving over the same spot) dropping a localized 5-7 inches of rain while Boone recieved just under 3. No notable damage was reported from the Blowing Rock area, although there was one report of a small amount of water on a ground floor. Wet Summer... For Some Meteorological summer spans the months of June, July, and August, meaning we can now look back on the season as a whole. While temperatures were above normal (but not by a significant margin), precipitation varied by location. This should not come as a surprise, as the vast majority of summertime precipitation comes from afternoon & evening showers & thunderstorms, which are incredibly hit-or-miss. A few miles difference can mean a few inches of rain, which adds up over the course of a summer. Typically, far southwestern North Carolina tends to be the wettest place not only in the state, but in the entire Eastern US. This was not the case this summer, as the maps below show. The first map shows the departure from normal for June 1st to August 31st. Look down near Nantahala National Forest and Brevard, where multiple stations were over 6 inches below average on summer precipitation. Conversely, most stations along and north of Interstate 40 were 2 to 4 inches above average. Highlands, Brevard, Waynesville, and Cullowhee falling shy of Boone's summer total is not something we see often. Highlands recieving less than Asheville is even more surprising, given that Asheville lies in one of the driest areas of the state, the French Broad River Valley, while Highlands lies in a rainforest averaging nearly 90 inches of rain per year. The map below shows total precipitation for the summer. Year-to-date precipitation totals are still behind schedule at all locations in our region... except Marshall in Madison County, which is an inch ahead. Much of Avery County as well as Brevard and Highlands are over 10 inches below what the average year-to-date precipitation should be through the end of August. The Foothills lie 6 to 10 inches behind. Given the El Niño conditions, the late fall and winter period may bring an opportunity to recoup some of that. But, September does not tend to be an especially wet month unless a tropical system moves through, and the tropics have been very quiet thus far. We are approaching the modern record for the deepest run into a year without a storm reaching hurricane strength (the record - Sept. 11th, dating back over 60 years). Looks Like Summer Our monthly bar graph feature for August goes to North Wilkesboro, where temperatures were about where you'd expect them to be in the afternoons. North Wilkesboro did manage to go 31 for 31 on high temperatures at or above 80 degrees (not unusual - the average is 27 days above 80), but only 5 days surpassed 90 degrees, 3 below average. A far cry from last August, which had a remarkable 14 days with high temperatures below 80 degrees. Minimum temperatures were more notably above normal, with 15 lows of 70 or greater and only 1 low below 60 degrees. Temperatures Monthly mean temperatures were above average across the board. The only exceptions on above average lie with a handful of stations that managed below average mean high temperature for the month (Jefferson, Sparta, and Marshall), but low temperatures were above average without exception. Averaging everything out showed generally 1 to 4 degrees above average, again mostly thanks to warm low temperatures. Town by town specifics lie below.

A handful of stations failed to reach their average, but only one fell shy of 80% of it - Mount Mitchell, where average is 7.69". The percentage winner in the table below is Lenoir, where average precip was more than doubled this August.
